accuracy.evidence: Animal body-language cues match RSPCA and Blue Cross guidance for children around cats and dogs: purring and leaning in mean the cat is comfortable; flattened ears, a swishing tail and walking away mean stop and give it space; stroke slowly along the back rather than patting hard. Minibeast homes (worms in soil, snails under leaves, ladybirds on flowers and plants) match RHS and Wildlife Trusts guidance to return creatures to where they were found. EYFS links (PSED building relationships and managing self; Understanding the World: The Natural World) were checked against the 2024 statutory framework and Development Matters.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets what three- and four-year-olds actually do: excited fast, hard patting (the stroke speed test and first prediction), following or picking up a pet that has walked off (second prediction and the 'Pick it up' challenge option), keeping a minibeast in a jar or pocket as a pet (third prediction and the jar drop zone), picking flowers or stamping on plants, and grabbing toys instead of asking.

lab_distinct.evidence: The lab measures how the child moves: the cat stroke is scored on drag speed and length, so a slow stroke earns a purr and a fast swipe makes the cat run. The other steps read an animal's body signals, return minibeasts to habitat zones with a jar decoy, care for a plant that grows or droops, and choose kind words with a friend. No other flagship lab scores the speed of a gesture; it passed the 30% shingle gate.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child feels the difference between gentle and rough before being told, then learns that gentle includes stopping when the animal says no, then extends gentle care to minibeasts and plants (living things), and finally to people through please, thank you, are you OK and sorry, matching the topic's evidence statements (strokes a pet gently, puts a minibeast back, uses kind words).

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting wrong options that the lab then answers: 'pat hard and fast: purr and stay' (the cat runs), 'the cat walks away: pick it up' (let it go), and 'a snail on the path: keep it in a jar' (the jar is not a home; the snail goes back on the leaves).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating questions with eleven distinct m= messages that name the slip: fast and hard strokes, pulling a tail, squashing a worm, a pocket is not a home, stroking more after flat ears, picking up a cat that says leave me be, shouting for a turn, pushing, picking a park flower, and stamping on it.

readability.evidence: Kid text is very short read-aloud sentences with concrete things (cat, worm, snail, ladybird, plant) within the family kid limit; canvas instructions are one line and every tap target pairs a large emoji with one or two words. Adult text names EYFS areas and body-language cues within the adult limit.

no_filler.evidence: Passed the filler regex and the 12% duplicate gate. Kid paragraphs cover what gentle means, pets and stop signs, minibeasts, and plants plus kind words; adult paragraphs cover the EYFS areas, how to teach gentle touch and read animal signals, named mistakes, and what the lab does.

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 px screenshots of every step at start and after Show me in both themes: the cat and hearts are centred, the three cat-answer cards and the soil, leaves and flower homes fit in one row with the jar at the end of the path, plant tools fit in one row with short labels (and full buttons below), and both speech bubbles are full width; the minibeast title clipping and long plant labels were fixed after the first screenshots.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs: axe WCAG 2.1 AA clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13, every task completed with Show me, no console errors. Every drag or tap has a button route (slow stroke / fast pat, stroke softly / stop / let it go, minibeast-to-home buttons, plant care buttons, both speech bubbles), and the canvas aria-label states the instruction and what happened after each move.
